note: Seed batch for PulseRoom 2.0. Written to the final schema so the engine, visuals and voice can be built against real content.

questions.q: My kick and 808 are fighting. How do I fix it?
questions.short: Decide which one owns the sub, then carve the other out of its way.
steps: Pick the role: 808 owns 30-60 Hz, kick owns 60-100 Hz (usual choice), or swap it for a kick-led record.
High-pass the kick at 40-50 Hz so it stops competing below the 808.
Sidechain the 808 to the kick: 2-4 dB of ducking, 10 ms attack, release timed to the kick's decay.
Tune the 808 to the song key — an out-of-key 808 will never sit, no matter the EQ.
questions.why: Two sources with energy in the same octave sum into mud and cancel each other's definition. Separating them by role rather than level is what makes both audible at once.
questions.watch: Heavy ducking that pumps the whole track usually means the release is too slow.

genreNotes.hiphop: Trap records often let the 808 own everything below 100 Hz and use the kick purely as a transient click on top.
genreNotes.amapiano: The log drum is the bass instrument — treat it as the 808 here and keep the kick short and high.

questions.q: I only have a few vocal takes. How do I build a stack?
aliases: make one vocal sound like many
questions.short: Build width from timing and pitch differences, never from copies of the identical file.
steps: Duplicate the take, nudge one copy 12-25 ms late, pan the pair hard left and right.
Pitch one copy up 8 cents and the other down 8 cents so they beat against each other.
Give each copy slightly different EQ — one brighter, one darker — so they stop sounding like one source.
Drop both 5-8 dB under the original and high-pass them at 150 Hz.
Check in mono. If it hollows out, reduce the delay offset to under 15 ms.
questions.why: A duplicated file panned apart is still one mono signal and collapses to the centre. Small timing and pitch differences are what the ear reads as two separate singers.
questions.watch: Offsets past 30 ms stop sounding like a double and start sounding like a slapback echo.

genreNotes.gospel: Real stacked takes always beat this. Use it to thicken an existing stack, not to replace a session.
genreNotes.afrobeats: Ad-libs respond especially well — treat each ad-lib as its own narrow pair rather than widening the lead.

questions.q: My choir is swallowing the lead vocal. What do I do?
questions.short: Carve the choir around the lead instead of turning the choir down.
steps: High-pass the choir higher than the lead — 150-200 Hz — so it stops competing for chest.
Dip the choir 2-3 dB at 3-5 kHz, exactly where the lead's presence lives.
Compress the choir harder than the lead, 4:1 and 4-8 dB, so it becomes one flat texture.
Give the choir a longer reverb than the lead, which places it behind without lowering it.
Only now adjust the fader, and expect to move it less than you thought.
questions.why: Two voices in the same frequency range mask each other, so lowering the choir only makes the arrangement smaller without making the lead clearer. Removing the overlap keeps both present.
questions.watch: Cutting the choir's top end too hard makes consonants mush. Dip the presence region, not the air above 10 kHz.

genreNotes.gospel: When the choir is the moment rather than the backing, invert this: duck the lead's reverb and let the choir take the presence band.

questions.q: My whole mix sounds muddy. Where do I start?
questions.short: Mud is usually too many instruments sharing 200-500 Hz, not one bad channel.
steps: High-pass everything that is not kick, bass or a full-range pad — guitars at 100 Hz, keys at 120 Hz, pads at 150 Hz.
Find the two or three instruments that need 200-500 Hz most and let them keep it; cut 2-3 dB there on everything else.
Check how many sources are playing at once in that range — the fix is often arrangement, not EQ.
Only touch the mix bus after the channels are clean, and then never more than 1-1.5 dB.
questions.why: Every instrument has some energy at 200-500 Hz. Individually fine, together it sums into a wall that masks everything above it. Cutting a little on many channels beats cutting a lot on one.
questions.watch: If the mix turns thin and brittle, you cut too widely — restore the instruments that carry the song's warmth.

genreNotes.highlife: Several guitars plus horns plus organ all crowd the low mids. Assign each a lane: rhythm guitar high, organ low, horns in between.
genreNotes.gospel: A live band plus choir plus organ is the hardest case — the organ is usually the one to carve, not the voices.

questions.q: My reverb is making the mix muddy. How do I fix it?
questions.short: Filter the reverb return and shorten the tail before you lower the send.
steps: Put an EQ on the reverb return, not the source.
High-pass the return at 200-300 Hz so the tail stops adding low mids.
Low-pass at 8-10 kHz so it stops adding hiss and sibilance.
Shorten the decay so the tail ends before the next phrase — at 120 BPM that is about 1.5 s.
Add pre-delay of 20-40 ms to separate the word from its tail.
questions.why: Most reverb mud comes from low frequencies in the tail, which pile up under everything. Filtering the return keeps the sense of space while removing the part that clouds the mix.
questions.watch: If filtering makes it sound small, shorten the decay instead of opening the filters back up.

genreNotes.gospel: A room with a live band already has natural ambience — you usually need far less added reverb than a programmed record.

questions.q: How do I mix an 808 so it translates everywhere?
questions.short: Saturate it so there are harmonics above the sub, because small speakers cannot reproduce the fundamental.
steps: Tune the 808 to the song key first — everything else is wasted if the pitch is wrong.
High-pass at 25-30 Hz to remove rumble you cannot hear but that eats headroom.
Add saturation or distortion, and listen at 500 Hz - 2 kHz for the harmonics appearing.
Compress gently, 4:1 with 15-30 ms attack, 2-5 dB, so every note sits at the same level.
Keep everything below 120 Hz mono.
questions.why: Phone and laptop speakers cannot reproduce 40 Hz at all. Saturation creates harmonics an octave or two up, and the ear reconstructs the missing fundamental from them — which is why a saturated 808 is audible on a phone and a pure sine is silent.
questions.watch: Too much distortion turns the 808 into a buzzing mid-range instrument. Blend the distorted copy under the clean one if it gets aggressive.

genreNotes.afrobeats: The log drum needs the same treatment but keep it shorter and more percussive than a trap 808.
genreNotes.amapiano: The log drum is the hook — saturate it hard and let it be the brightest low-end element.

questions.q: How do I mix highlife guitars so they don't clash?
questions.short: Give each guitar its own frequency lane and its own side of the stereo field.
steps: High-pass every guitar at 100-150 Hz; none of them need low end in this arrangement.
Pan the interlocking parts opposite each other, 50-80% left and right.
Carve complementary EQ: lift 2-3 kHz on one, 4-5 kHz on the other, and cut where you lifted on the opposite part.
Keep compression light, 3:1 and 2-3 dB — the picking dynamics are the groove.
Add a short 1/8 or 1/16 delay on one side only to widen without doubling.
questions.why: Highlife guitar parts interlock rhythmically in the same register. Panning separates them in space and complementary EQ separates them in tone, so the listener hears the conversation between them instead of a blur.
questions.watch: Do not high-pass so hard that the guitars lose the woody body that defines the style.

genreNotes.highlife: The lead guitar is a melodic voice, almost a second singer — give it presence around 3 kHz and automate it like a vocal.

questions.q: How do I make a piano sound wide and big?
questions.short: Width comes from the recording's natural spread and from space, not from a stereo widener.
steps: If it is a stereo recording, keep it stereo and avoid any mono-summing plugin.
High-pass at 80-120 Hz so the left hand stops competing with the bass.
Cut 2-3 dB at 250-400 Hz where the body turns to mud in a full arrangement.
Add a stereo reverb with 25-35 ms pre-delay; the early reflections are what read as size.
Keep everything below 150 Hz mono so the low notes stay solid.
questions.why: A piano is already a wide source because the strings are physically spread. Most narrowness comes from the arrangement crowding it, so making room is more effective than artificially widening.
questions.watch: Stereo wideners on a piano often destroy mono compatibility — check in mono before keeping one.

genreNotes.gospel: When piano and organ play together, keep the piano above 150 Hz and let the organ hold the low register, or they turn to soup.

questions.q: What is pre-delay and what should I set it to?
questions.short: Pre-delay is the gap before the reverb starts, and it is what keeps words clear inside a big space.
steps: Start at 20-40 ms for vocals — enough to separate the word from its tail.
Sync it to the song: a 1/64 note at your tempo is a reliable starting point.
More pre-delay makes the source sound closer and the space bigger.
Less pre-delay glues the source into the space, which suits pads and strings.
Zero pre-delay on a vocal is what makes it sound like it is singing from inside a cave.
questions.why: Your ear locates a sound by its first arrival and judges the room by what follows. Separating the two lets the brain hear a close singer in a large room, rather than a distant singer.
questions.watch: Pre-delay longer than about 80 ms starts to be heard as a distinct slapback rather than a room.

questions.q: What is masking and how do I hear it?
aliases: why can't I hear an instrument
questions.short: Masking is one sound hiding another because they share the same frequency range at the same moment.
steps: Solo the two suspects together, then mute each in turn — if one gets clearer when the other stops, they are masking.
Sweep a narrow boost on the less important source to find where the overlap is loudest.
Cut there on the less important source rather than boosting on the more important one.
Check whether the two parts actually need to play at the same time — arrangement solves masking better than EQ.
questions.why: The ear has limited resolution within a frequency band. When two sources fill the same band, the louder one wins and the quieter one is perceived as absent rather than quiet, which is why turning it up rarely fixes it.
questions.watch: Chasing masking with boosts makes every element louder and the mix smaller. Cut, do not boost.

questions.q: Should my low end be mono?
questions.short: Yes, below roughly 120 Hz — stereo low end falls apart on club systems and phones.
steps: Put a mono-maker or mid/side EQ on the mix bus and set it to collapse everything below 120-150 Hz.
Check the mix in mono and listen for the bass changing level — that means phase problems.
Keep kick and bass dead centre; width belongs to everything above them.
Test on a phone speaker, which is mono, before deciding you are finished.
questions.why: Low frequencies have long wavelengths, so stereo differences down there are mostly phase differences. Played on a mono system they cancel, and the bass can simply disappear.
questions.watch: Collapsing too high, above about 200 Hz, starts to narrow instruments that should stay wide.

genreNotes.amapiano: Club playback is the target — be strict about this one.
genreNotes.afrobeats: Most listening is on phones, which are mono; the low end has to survive the collapse.

questions.q: How do I glue my drums together?
questions.short: Light bus compression plus saturation, with the individual drums already balanced.
steps: Balance the kit with faders first — bus processing cannot fix a bad balance.
Bus compressor: 2:1 to 4:1, 10-30 ms attack, auto release, 2-4 dB of gain reduction.
Add tape or console saturation after the compressor to round the transient peaks.
Blend a heavily crushed parallel copy underneath for energy, 10:1 and 10-20 dB, at 10-20% of the level.
Compare bypassed at matched loudness — if it is not clearly better, you overdid it.
questions.why: Compressing the whole kit together makes the quiet elements move with the loud ones, which is the physical reason a kit sounds like one performance rather than separate samples.
questions.watch: If the cymbals pump when the kick hits, the attack is too fast or the ratio too high.

genreNotes.gospel: Live kits glue more easily because the room mics already share a space — use less compression than you would on programmed drums.
genreNotes.hiphop: Programmed drums need more help; parallel crush is doing most of the work.

questions.q: How do I mix a Hammond organ in gospel?
questions.short: The organ fills every gap by nature, so carve it hard and let it be the bed, not the feature.
steps: High-pass at 100-120 Hz unless the organ is holding the bass line.
Cut 3-4 dB at 250-400 Hz — this is where the organ buries everything else.
Keep the Leslie's stereo spread but check it in mono for phase cancellation.
Compress lightly, 2:1 and 2-3 dB; heavy compression kills the swell of the drawbars.
Automate it down under the vocal and up in the turnarounds.
questions.why: A Hammond played with full drawbars is close to a full-spectrum pad. In a dense arrangement it masks the piano, the guitars and the lower part of the voices at once, so it needs more carving than almost any other instrument.
questions.watch: Do not high-pass a bass-pedal organ part — check what register the player is actually in first.

genreNotes.gospel: During the vamp the organ becomes a lead instrument. Automate the carve away in those sections instead of leaving it static.

questions.q: My mix sounds good on headphones but bad in the car. Why?
questions.short: You mixed to one system's flattery; translation comes from checking several and from mid-range balance.
steps: Check on three systems: headphones, a phone speaker, and one more, before judging anything.
If it vanishes on the phone, your information is all below 200 Hz — add harmonics with saturation.
If it is harsh in the car, you were mixing quietly on headphones; check at conversation level on speakers.
Loudness-match against two reference tracks in the same genre and compare the mid-range.
Mix mostly at low volume — balance decisions made loud do not survive.
questions.why: Every system reproduces a different slice of the spectrum. A mix that depends on one slice fails on the others, whereas a mix with the important information in the mid-range survives everywhere, because every speaker reproduces the mid-range.
questions.watch: Do not EQ for one bad system. Fix what is wrong on all of them.

genreNotes.afrobeats: Phone playback dominates — if the hook does not work on a phone speaker it does not work.
